scientificSummary.scope: A bounded immune-mediated podocytopathy map of primary minimal change nephropathy: anti-nephrin autoantibodies with humoral and Th2 associations, T-cell and cytokine (IL-8, IL-13) observations, experimental antibody and IL-13 models, foot-process effacement and nephrotic syndrome. Excludes secondary causes, genetics, other glomerulopathies and treatment efficacy; CD80, CTLA-4 and ANGPTL4 evidence is not yet curated.

paragraphs.text: Within this bounded map, primary minimal change disease (MCD) is represented as an immune-associated podocytopathy in which diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement accompanies nephrotic-range proteinuria, with heterogeneous upstream pathogenesis. The best-supported mechanism in the map involves circulating autoantibodies against nephrin, a structural and signalling protein of the podocyte slit diaphragm. In a multicentre cohort, anti-nephrin antibodies were detected in 44% of adults with MCD and 69% of those with active untreated disease; independent cohorts using different assays found comparable subset-level positivity. Antibody levels tracked disease activity and proteinuria, fell during remission, reappeared before relapse, and correlated with podocyte-associated punctate IgG in biopsies. Experimentally, nephrin immunization in mice induced an MCD-like nephrotic syndrome with slit-diaphragm IgG, nephrin phosphorylation and severe podocyte cytoskeletal changes, and passive transfer of patient IgG to a rabbit caused proteinuria, foot-process effacement without deposits and increased nephrin tyrosine phosphorylation. Together these support a pathogenic antibody-mediated mechanism in a subset of patients, in which antibody binding at the slit diaphragm alters nephrin signalling and podocyte architecture, leading to effacement and albumin leakage. Anti-nephrin-positive patients also showed a non-significant trend toward more plasmablasts, an IgG4-predominant subclass and a Th2-skewed serum cytokine profile, linking humoral and Th2 findings without establishing their sequence.

Substantial uncertainty remains. Antibody prevalence is cohort- and assay-dependent, the initiating immune events are undefined, and the mechanism of antibody-negative disease is unresolved. The intracellular sequence from antibody binding through phosphorylation and cytoskeletal change to effacement has not been established, and the passive-transfer evidence rests on IgG from one patient given to one rabbit. Peripheral CD4 T-cell expansion with CD69 activation at onset remains a human association, not an established initiating cause or a universal T-cell-derived permeability factor. IL-13 overexpression in rats produced foot-process fusion, nephrin downregulation and B7-1 upregulation, showing experimental sufficiency rather than human necessity. Urinary IL-8 rose during relapse, but the same study concluded that IL-8 and TNF-alpha may not play a disease-specific pathogenic role; that negative finding is limited to its tested conditions and does not exclude context-dependent cytokine effects. Multiple immune pathways may therefore converge on podocyte dysfunction, and no single upstream defect is established as necessary or sufficient for all primary MCD. Spontaneous remission and relapse in an individual case illustrate clinical variability without identifying a mechanism. Concurrent antibody clearance and steroid-induced remission do not show that antibody reduction alone explains treatment benefit; treatment efficacy is not synthesized here. Most evidence was inspected at abstract level and awaits independent domain review.

scientificSummary.scope: A bounded immune-mediated podocytopathy map of primary minimal change nephropathy: anti-nephrin autoantibodies with humoral and Th2 associations, observational hemopexin activity, T-cell and cytokine (IL-8, IL-13) observations, experimental antibody and IL-13 models, foot-process effacement and nephrotic syndrome. Excludes secondary causes, genetics, other glomerulopathies and treatment efficacy; CD80, CTLA-4 and ANGPTL4 evidence is not yet curated.

paragraphs.text: Primary minimal change disease (MCD) is represented here as an immune-associated podocytopathy with heterogeneous upstream pathogenesis, foot-process effacement and nephrotic proteinuria. Anti-nephrin autoantibodies identify a subset: one multicentre cohort detected them in 44% of adults with MCD and 69% with active untreated disease. Levels tracked activity and proteinuria, fell during remission and reappeared before relapse; human antibody detection remains quantitatively inconsistent. A cell-based assay cohort detected antibodies in 7/36 adults with MCD (19.44%); another pediatric/young-adult cohort found 15% MCD and 11% FSGS positivity. Anti-nephrin is neither universal nor specific to MCD. Human biopsy findings associate antibodies with podocyte IgG. Nephrin immunization in mice induced an MCD-like syndrome, nephrin phosphorylation and podocyte cytoskeletal changes. Patient IgG transferred to a rabbit caused proteinuria, effacement without deposits and nephrin phosphorylation. These experiments demonstrate injury in selected models; human assay results do not establish a settled causal mechanism or explain antibody-negative disease. Anti-nephrin-positive patients also had IgG4 predominance, Th2-skewed cytokines and a non-significant plasmablast trend; their sequence is unresolved. A human study found higher hemopexin protease activity despite lower hemopexin concentration during MCD relapse, compared with remission. This supplies a separate observational circulating-factor signal, not proof that hemopexin causes human MCD.

A two-cohort methodology study found method- and antigen-dependent false positives and negatives: approximately half of 24 MCD samples had weak signals detectable only by immunoprecipitation-Western blotting, while strong cross-assay signals occurred in two FSGS samples. Assay standardization and orthogonal confirmation therefore matter; human seropositivity cannot be equated with pathogenic antibody activity. The rabbit experiment used total IgG from one patient in one recipient, rather than purified nephrin-specific antibody. The hemopexin comparison included 18 relapsing patients and 23 in post-prednisolone remission, leaving treatment and stage confounding; its tissue assay did not establish in vivo causation. Peripheral CD4 activation remains associative. IL-13 overexpression caused albuminuria, effacement and nephrin/B7-1 changes in rats; effects remain model-dependent, not uniformly pathogenic or necessary in humans. Urinary IL-8 rose in relapse, yet the same report did not support a disease-specific IL-8/TNF-alpha role under tested conditions. No upstream factor is established as universal. Concurrent steroid-induced remission and antibody clearance do not isolate a treatment mediator. Secondary causes, other glomerulopathies and treatment efficacy are excluded. Human and animal graph contexts remain distinct; most sources were inspected at abstract level, with domain review and calibration pending.

after.label: Hemopexin protease activity
after.description: Circulating hemopexin-associated protease activity measured in human MCD relapse and remission; observational evidence does not establish causal sufficiency.

after.text: Plasma hemopexin protease activity was higher in patients with minimal change disease in relapse than in remission after prednisolone, and differed from selected other proteinuric diseases and healthy controls. This supports a circulating-factor hypothesis without establishing hemopexin as a cause of human MCD.
limitations: Observational disease-state comparison with treatment differences and small comparator groups; temporal direction and causal sufficiency are not established.
The activity assay does not identify a universal circulating factor or establish that hemopexin causes all human MCD.
Lower measured hemopexin concentration coexisted with greater activity; abundance and protease activity must not be conflated.
